'''''Salvia microphylla''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] including '''''Salvia grahamii''''', '''''Salvia lemmonii''''' and '''''Salvia neurepia;'''''<ref name=POWO_30146334-2/> the '''baby sage''', '''Graham's sage''', or '''blackcurrant sage''', is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] found in the wild in southeastern Arizona and the mountains of eastern, western, and southern Mexico. It is a very complex species which easily hybridizes, resulting in numerous hybrids and cultivars brought into horticulture since the 1990s. The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''microphylla'', from the Greek, means "small leaved". In Mexico it is called ''mirto de montes'', or "myrtle of the mountains".<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book|last1=Clebsch|first1=Betsy|last2=Barner|first2=Carol D.|title=The New Book of Salvias|publisher=Timber Press|year=2003|pages=192–193|isbn=978-0-88192-560-9}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Baby Sage (Salvia microphylla).jpg|thumb|''S. microphylla'' 'Hot Lips']]
''Salvia microphylla'' grows to {{convert|1|to|1.3|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and wide, blooming in its first year and growing to full size in its second year. The leaves are ovate shaped, of varying sizes, and smooth or lightly covered with hairs. When crushed, the leaves have a strong fragrance, which has been described as pleasant and mint-like, but also as similar to that of [[blackcurrant]]s, leading to the use of "blackcurrant sage” as an English name for this species.<ref>See e.g. {{Citation |title=Norfolk Herbs online catalogue |url=http://www.norfolkherbs.co.uk/EnglishCatalogue/CatalogueS.html |access-date=20 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716191600/http://www.norfolkherbs.co.uk/EnglishCatalogue/CatalogueS.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=16 July 2011}}</ref> It sometimes spreads underground, producing dense patches.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

Along with its cultivars and hybrids, ''S. microphylla'' blooms heavily in late spring and again in autumn, with sporadic flowering year-round in mild conditions. The flowers are arranged in whorls, with a wide range of color: magenta, red, pink, and rose.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Mirto chico (Salvia microphylla) I.jpg|thumb|''S. microphylla'']]
Botanist [[Carl Epling]] considered ''Salvia microphylla'' to have three geographical races, though the wide variation still causes confusion today, and there are conceivably more than three races. Adding to the confusion, ''Salvia microphylla'' is often mistaken for ''[[Salvia greggii]]'', with which it frequently hybridizes. Epling distinguishes between the two by the ''S. microphylla'' leaves, which have serrated edges, compared to the narrow, elliptic, and smooth-edged ''S. greggii'' leaves — and by a pair of papillae inside the ''S. microphylla'' corolla.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

In the U.S. it is sometimes called "Graham's sage," as it was named ''Salvia grahamii'' by [[George Bentham]]. It was also named ''Salvia neurepia'' by [[Merritt Lyndon Fernald]]. {{As of|2024|April}}, both these scientific names were considered to be synonyms of ''Salvia microphylla''.<ref name=POWO_30146334-2/>

There has also been confusion between ''Salvia microphylla'' and ''Salvia lemmonii'', which was named by [[Asa Gray]]. Later, Gray began calling it ''Salvia microphylla'' var. ''wislizeni'', considering it to be a variety of ''S. microphylla''.<ref name="Clebsch"/> {{As of|2024|April}},  ''Salvia lemmonii'' was considered to be a synonym of ''Salvia microphylla''.<ref name=POWO_30146334-2/>

===Proposed varieties===
Varieties of ''Salvia microphylla'' that have been proposed include the following, although all were regarded as synonymous with the species by Plants of the World Online {{as of|2024|April|lc=yes}}:
*''S. microphylla'' var. ''canescens'' <small>A.Gray</small>
*''S. microphylla'' var. ''neurepia'' <small>(Fernald) Epling</small>
*''S. microphylla'' var. ''wislizeni'' <small>A.Gray</small>

==Cultivars and hybrids==
[[File:Salvia microphylla neurepia.jpg|thumb|''Salvia microphylla'' 'Forever Red']]
Some cultivars are hybrids with ''Salvia greggii'' (known as ''Salvia'' × ''jamensis'') and other ''Salvia'' species; collectively they may be called "Mexican salvias".<ref name=Dyso15>{{citation |mode=cs1 |last=Dyson |first=William |date=September 2015 |title=RHS trial of Mexican ''Salvia'' |journal=The Plantsman |series=New Series |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=158–164 }}</ref> Technically they are evergreen shrubs or sub-shrubs, though they are not reliably hardy and are also short-lived. However, they are easy to propagate from [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]]. Those marked <small>AGM</small> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 94 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 12 October 2018}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Salvia microphylla'' is grown in central Mexico as a medicinal plant, and used for making tea.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hanelt|first1=Peter|last2=Büttner|first2=R.|last3=Mansfeld|first3=Rudolf|last4=Kilian|first4=Ruth|title=Mansfeld's Encyclopedia of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops|publisher=Springer|year=2001|pages=2022|isbn=978-3-540-41017-1}}</ref>
